title: Customer Support Agent with Human-Approved Refunds
summary: Hybrid workflow: code owns routing, policy and money; the model classifies, drafts cited replies and proposes refunds. Every refund is an exact, single-use, human-approved action.
autonomy: Level: hybrid workflow (Ch1 autonomy dial, Ch24). The model may choose wording and propose a route; it can never authorize or execute a refund. Read-only and drafting are automatic, refunds are human-approved, anything unclear escalates.
key_decisions: Hybrid workflow, not a free agent: money moves only through code (Ch24)
Approve the exact refund, single-use and expiring, never the agent (Ch49)
Read-only first, drafts next, bounded writes last (Ch56)
One agent is enough: no multi-agent split (Ch31)
Retrieved text and emails are data, never instructions (Ch47)
Release only when the eval gate says PROMOTE (Ch45)
rationale: Workflow vs agent: refunds are irreversible, so routing, eligibility and execution live in deterministic code; the model only classifies and drafts (Ch24, Ch1).
Single agent: no measured shortfall justifies more agents; every boundary adds cost, latency and failure points (Ch31).
Durable interrupt: the graph checkpoints before the approval pause and resumes without repeating finished steps; the interrupted node has no side effects (Ch23, Ch19).
Tools: narrow MCP servers with separate read and write scopes, a client-side allowlist that fails closed, and authorization in the host, not the protocol (Ch11, Ch29, Ch28).
Grounding: hybrid retrieval with metadata filters; replies cite policy IDs or abstain with a handoff (Ch17, Ch20).
Memory: no long-term memory in v1. Case state lives in checkpoints; add owner-scoped preferences later only through approval (Ch18, Ch19).
trust_boundaries: Channel to API: authenticate the customer, validate a typed request, attach request_id (Ch51).
Retrieved passages and customer text to model: labelled as untrusted data with provenance (Ch9, Ch47).
Model proposal to refund tool: policy gate (deny by default) plus a keyed, single-use human approval receipt bound to tool, target and amount (Ch48, Ch49).
Host to MCP servers: caller-side allowlist and scoped tokens; tokens are never passed through to downstream services (Ch28, Ch29).
failure_handling: Every tool call has a timeout and returns a structured error envelope; only transient errors are retried, with a cap and backoff (Ch14, Ch53).
Refund writes carry an idempotency key from business facts (order_id + amount + reason); a lost response is checked against the ledger before any retry (Ch14, Ch53).
Named stop reasons: MODEL_ANSWER, STEP_BUDGET, TOKEN_BUDGET, ESCALATED, DENIED. Anything but MODEL_ANSWER is incomplete work (Ch14).
Approval timeout or missing reviewer fails toward no refund and escalation, never execution (Ch49).
Circuit breaker on the refund provider; compensation is a new, separately approved action (Ch53).
hitl: Every refund: reviewer sees order, policy citation, amount and draft, then approves one exact action (Ch49).
Over-limit, unclear intent, policy conflict or abstention: escalate to a human queue (Ch56).
evals: Golden set with stable case IDs: happy paths, ineligible refunds, over-limit, injection in email body, missing order (Ch42).
Separate dimensions: task success, groundedness (cited policy IDs), tool accuracy, safety (zero unapproved refunds), trajectory efficiency (Ch41).
Trace every run as one span tree; release gate PROMOTE/HOLD with a zero-tolerance safety floor (Ch43, Ch45, Ch65).
risks: Prompt injection in emails steering refunds: mitigated by the policy gate and approval; owner: support platform lead (Ch46).
Reviewer rubber-stamping: show evidence, sample audits, track approval latency; owner: support ops manager (Ch49, Ch59).
Policy drift making KB stale: version sources, re-index on change (Ch16).
non_goals: Account changes or cancellations in v1
